Why your take-home is so much less than your CTC

CTC (Cost to Company) is the total annual cost your employer bears for you — and it includes several components you never see in your bank account. The gap between CTC and in-hand typically ranges from 20% to 35% depending on salary level, city, and tax regime.

The biggest components eating into your CTC: Employer's PF contribution (12% of basic salary) is part of your CTC but goes directly to your EPF account — you can't spend it monthly. Income tax is deducted at source (TDS) every month based on your projected annual tax liability. Employee's PF contribution (another 12% of basic) is deducted from your gross salary. Professional tax (₹200/month in most states) is a small but mandatory state-level deduction. The rest of CTC that reaches your bank is your in-hand salary.

New regime vs old regime — a real comparison with numbers

For FY 2025-26, the new tax regime is the default. Here's how to think about which one saves you more tax:

New regime advantages: Lower tax slab rates across the board. Standard deduction of ₹75,000. Full rebate under Section 87A if taxable income is ₹7 lakh or less (meaning zero tax for most people earning under ₹7.75 lakh CTC). No paperwork for deductions — simpler filing.

Old regime advantages: Allows HRA exemption (saves significant tax for metro city renters), 80C deductions up to ₹1.5 lakh (PF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance, home loan principal), 80D deductions for health insurance, home loan interest under Section 24, and several other exemptions.

Practical rule of thumb: If your total deductions and exemptions under the old regime (HRA + 80C + 80D + others) exceed roughly ₹3.5–4 lakh, the old regime likely saves you more tax. Below that threshold, the new regime's lower rates usually win. For someone in a metro paying ₹20,000/month rent with full 80C investment and health insurance, the old regime often wins at CTC levels of ₹10–20 lakh. Use the toggle above to compare both — the calculator shows the tax under each regime live.

How your CTC is typically structured

This calculator uses a standard Indian corporate salary structure. Most private sector companies in India split CTC roughly as: Basic salary at 40–50% of CTC (the foundation for PF, gratuity, and other calculations). HRA at 40–50% of basic (50% for metro cities, 40% for non-metro, as per Income Tax rules). LTA (Leave Travel Allowance) at approximately one month's basic per year. Special allowance absorbs the remaining CTC after the above components.

Actual structures vary significantly by employer. Startups often have simpler structures (higher special allowance, lower PF-linked components). Government and PSU salary structures follow different rules (DA, TA, grade pay). Consulting firms may have variable pay components. This calculator works best for standard private sector salaried employment.

Components that appear in CTC but not in your payslip's gross

Employer's PF contribution (12% of basic) — included in CTC, deposited in your EPF account, not in your bank. You can access this when you leave the job or retire, subject to EPF withdrawal rules.

Gratuity — usually 4.81% of basic, accrues over your tenure and is paid as a lump sum when you complete 5 years or leave. Often included in CTC projections even though you only receive it conditionally. This calculator doesn't separate gratuity — check your offer letter to see if it's included in your quoted CTC.

Variable pay / performance bonus — commonly 10–20% of fixed CTC at mid-to-senior levels. This calculator covers only fixed CTC. Variable pay is taxable in the year it's paid and will increase your actual annual tax.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my actual take-home different from this calculator?

Several reasons: your employer's actual CTC structure may differ from the standard split used here (basic % varies widely), your company may have additional deductions (group health insurance premium, meal cards, transport), your professional tax may differ from ₹2,400/year (varies by state — Maharashtra is ₹2,500, Karnataka is ₹2,400, many states don't have it at all), or you have TDS deducted based on actual investment proofs submitted. Use this calculator for estimation and planning — always refer to your actual payslip for exact figures.

What is the Section 87A rebate and who gets it?

Section 87A provides a full income tax rebate (zero tax) for individuals whose net taxable income does not exceed ₹7 lakh under the new regime (₹5 lakh under the old regime). This means if your taxable income after standard deduction is ₹7 lakh or less under the new regime, your total income tax liability is ₹0 — regardless of which slab would otherwise apply. For most salaried employees with CTC up to approximately ₹7.75–8 lakh, the effective tax burden is zero under the new regime.

Is PF deduction mandatory?

If your basic salary is ₹15,000/month or less, PF deduction is mandatory by law. Above ₹15,000, technically only ₹1,800/month (12% of ₹15,000) is the minimum mandatory employer contribution, but most companies deduct PF on actual basic salary. Some companies (especially startups) allow you to opt out of PF above the statutory ceiling — this increases your take-home but reduces your retirement savings and the associated tax benefits. There's no universal right answer; it depends on whether you'll invest the extra take-home productively.

How is HRA exemption calculated?

HRA exemption under the old regime is the minimum of three values: (1) actual HRA received, (2) actual rent paid minus 10% of basic salary, (3) 50% of basic salary for metro cities or 40% for non-metro. You need rent receipts and the landlord's PAN if annual rent exceeds ₹1 lakh to claim this. Under the new regime, HRA exemption is not available — HRA is fully taxable as part of your salary, which is a major reason the old regime often wins for metro-city renters.
